final_proof:
Let A = {0} ∪ s[P]. Since s is a mapping from P to P, its image s[P] is a subset of P; also 0 ∈ P. Hence A ⊆ P. We have 0 ∈ A. Moreover, A is closed under s: if x ∈ A, then x ∈ P, and therefore s(x) ∈ s[P] ⊆ A. The induction axiom of the Peano structure now applies to A and gives A = P. Thus P = {0} ∪ s[P].

Another defining axiom of a Peano structure says that 0 is not a successor, i.e. 0 ∉ s[P]. We now prove the desired set equality directly. If x ∈ P ∖ s[P], then, because P = {0} ∪ s[P], either x = 0 or x ∈ s[P]. The latter alternative contradicts x ∉ s[P], so x = 0. Hence P ∖ s[P] ⊆ {0}. Conversely, 0 ∈ P and 0 ∉ s[P], so 0 ∈ P ∖ s[P], and consequently {0} ⊆ P ∖ s[P]. Therefore P ∖ s[P] = {0}, which is a singleton. In particular, 0 is the unique element of P that is not in the image of s, and hence is the unique non-successor element.
